cards.def: During the Ice Age, hunters from Asia followed big game across the Beringia land bridge or down the Pacific coast, so people first settled the Americas.
When that big game died out, the hunters' descendants in Mexico learned to farm squash, beans and maize, and the stored food let them build great cities like those of the Maya and Aztecs.
Because these farming peoples kept few domestic animals, they never caught animal-borne diseases like smallpox, so they had no immunity when Europeans finally arrived.
At the same time, across the ocean, a plague called the Black Death killed a quarter of Europe in the 1340s and 1350s, leaving survivors with more land and money to spend on ships and trade.

cards.term: 5. Europe wants a sea route to Asia (Ch. 2)
cards.def: With that new money, Europeans wanted to buy Asia's riches directly instead of paying Muslim traders in the middle, and to spread Christianity and win glory for their kings.
Searching for that sea route, Portugal built better ships and grew sugar on Atlantic islands with enslaved Africans, creating the plantation model later used in America.
Spain then sent Christopher Columbus west to reach Asia in 1492, but he landed in the Americas and connected the two separate worlds from cards 1 and 4.
Because Native Americans had no immunity (card 3), smallpox, Indian allies and Spanish guns let Hernán Cortés conquer the Aztecs, and their silver made Spain enormously rich.
Meanwhile Martin Luther's Reformation split Christians into Catholics and Protestants, so Protestant England saw Catholic Spain's American empire as a religious enemy to challenge.
To compete with Spain, Walter Raleigh started the Roanoke colony, but it failed because the colonists mistreated the local Indians and Spain's Armada cut off their supplies.
Spain protected its empire from rivals like England with Franciscan missions and soldiers in Florida and New Mexico, but forced labor and religious repression caused the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.
Learning from Roanoke's failure, England founded Jamestown in 1607, where settlers who would not farm survived only because Powhatan wanted their trade goods and guns.
John Rolfe's tobacco finally made Jamestown profitable, so planters brought indentured servants for land under the headright system and kept taking Powhatan land.
When tobacco prices fell under England's Navigation Acts, freed servants had no land, so in 1676 Nathaniel Bacon led them in rebellion against Governor Berkeley.
Frightened by Bacon's Rebellion, planters switched from servants to enslaved Africans and passed slave codes that united poor and rich whites against Black people.

cards.term: 16. The plantation model spreads to Carolina (Ch. 3)
cards.def: Sugar planters from Barbados carried this slave system to South Carolina to grow rice, and their trade in Indian slaves sparked the 1715 Yamasee War.
While England built plantations in the south, France under Samuel de Champlain built a fur-trading empire along the St. Lawrence, using Huron allies to trap beaver.
Fighting over those beaver furs, Iroquois armed with Dutch guns destroyed the Hurons, which pushed the French west toward the Mississippi.
Unlike the fur traders and the Chesapeake's single young men, Puritans fled England's religious persecution in families to build John Winthrop's godly "city upon a hill" in Massachusetts.
Shared faith and family life made New England stable, but it banished dissenters like Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, and its hunger for Indian land caused Metacom's War in 1675.

Between New England and the south, Dutch New York and William Penn's Quaker Pennsylvania mixed many peoples, and after the 1688 Glorious Revolution all these colonies were permanent, self-governing societies.
In the 1700s Spain and France still had few settlers, so Spain guarded Texas and California with forts and missions while New France relied on Indian allies.
British colonies instead grew fast through births, immigrants and slaves, but that growth split colonists by region and race, as the 1739 Stono slave rebellion showed.
Religion divided them further, as Benjamin Franklin's Enlightenment trusted human reason while George Whitefield's Great Awakening stirred emotional revivals that split churches.
Despite all these divisions, most white colonists were proud to be English because Britain's loose "benign neglect" gave them more land, chances and self-rule than people in England had.
